e-4949.worked_solution:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(4,8,2).$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 6 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14083796/assets/0589ebbdb2c14b93e1296b9e1f8b0caa0c3df49bff4c9fbb97e4c18102844ec1.png)

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|(-1)\cdot 2+6\cdot 4+4\cdot (-4)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-2+24-16|}{\sqrt{4+16+16}} \\  & =\frac{|\,6\,|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}

e-4950.knowledge_point: Finding the Shortest Distance Between a Point and a Plane Given in Simplified Dot Product Form
e-4950.problem: Given that $Q(1,-2,-1)$ lies on the plane $\Pi:\mathbf{r} \cdot \langle 2, 0, -2 \rangle = 4,$ find the shortest distance from $P(0 , -1 , 2)$ to $\Pi.$
e-4950.worked_solution:
First, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,-2,-1⟩-⟨0,-1,2⟩ \\  & =⟨1,-1,-3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the equation of a plane, we get a normal vector $\mathbf{n}= \langle 2, 0, -2 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|1\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|2+0+6|}{\sqrt{4+0+4}} \\  & =\frac{|\,8\,|}{\sqrt{8}} \\  & =\sqrt{8} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

e-4951.knowledge_point: Finding the Shortest Distance Between a Point and a Plane Given in Cartesian Form
e-4951.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(3 , -10 , 3)$ and the plane $\Pi$ with equation $2x+y-2z = -1$.
e-4951.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=4$ and $y=-5$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+y-2z & =-1 \\ 2(4)+(-5)+1 & =2z \\ 4 & =2z \\ z & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(4, -5, 2)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overrightarrow{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨4,-5,2⟩-⟨3,-10,3⟩ \\  & =⟨1,5,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $\mathbf{n}=\langle a,b,c \rangle.$ So, for the plane $\Pi,$ we have $\mathbf{n}= \langle 2, 1, -2 \rangle.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|1\cdot 2+5\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|2+5+2|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|\,9\,|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, Q(6,−1,5). Then

PQ→=⟨6,−1,5⟩−⟨−4,3,−1⟩=⟨10,−4,6⟩.

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector n=⟨−1,2,−2⟩.

Finally, the shortest distance from the point P to the plane Π is the absolute value of the scalar projection of PQ→ onto the normal vector of the plane:

d=|compnPQ→|=|PQ→⋅n||n|=|10⋅(−1)+(−4)⋅2+6⋅(−2)|(−1)2+22+(−2)2=|−10−8−12|1+4+4=|−30|9=303=10.

content.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-4,3,-1)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $(r-⟨6,-1,5⟩)\cdot ⟨-1,2,-2⟩=0.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(6,-1,5).$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨6,-1,5⟩-⟨-4,3,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨10,-4,6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector $n=⟨-1,2,-2⟩.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|10\cdot (-1)+(-4)\cdot 2+6\cdot (-2)|}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-10-8-12|}{\sqrt{1+4+4}} \\  & =\frac{|-30|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{30}{3} \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(2,0,-5)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $(r-[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=0.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(6,3,1).$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -5\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector $n=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|4\cdot 1+3\cdot 2+6\cdot 3|}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|4+6+18|}{\sqrt{1+4+9}} \\  & =\frac{|28|}{\sqrt{14}} \\  & =2\sqrt{14}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(1,2,-3)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $(r-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}])\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=0.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's pick a point on the plane, for instance, $Q(1,-2,1).$ Then 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Also, from the equation of the plane, we get a normal vector $n=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|0\cdot (-2)+(-4)\cdot 1+4\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4+8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\  & =\frac{|4|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+2y+z & =6 \\ -2(1)+2(1)+z & =6 \\ z & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,1,6)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,6⟩-⟨-1,4,-5⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,11⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨-2,2,1⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2+11\cdot 1|}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|-4-6+11|}{\sqrt{4+4+1}} \\  & =\frac{|1|}{\sqrt{9}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=1$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-4y+2z & =2 \\ 4(1)-4(1)+2z & =2 \\ 2z & =2 \\ z & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,1,1)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,1,1⟩-⟨-2,5,-3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-4,4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨4,-4,2⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|3\cdot 4+(-4)\cdot (-4)+4\cdot 2|}{\sqrt{{4}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|12+16+8|}{\sqrt{16+16+4}} \\  & =\frac{|36|}{\sqrt{36}} \\  & =\frac{36}{6} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for x and y into the equation and solve for z. Let's choose x=1 and y=0 (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for z, we get

6x+2y+3z=96(1)+2(0)+3z=93z=3z=1.

So, we get the point Q(1,0,1) which lies on the plane.

Computing PQ→, we get

PQ→=⟨1,0,1⟩−⟨−1,3,−4⟩=⟨2,−3,5⟩.

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane ax+by+cz=d, the normal vector is n=⟨a,b,c⟩. So, for the plane Π, we have n=⟨6,2,3⟩.

Finally, the shortest distance from the point P to the plane Π is the absolute value of the scalar projection of PQ→ onto the normal vector of the plane:

d=|compnPQ→|=|PQ→⋅n||n|=|2⋅6+(−3)⋅2+5⋅3|62+22+32=|12−6+15|36+4+9=|21|49=217=3.

content.problem: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-1,3,-4)$ and the plane $Π$ with equation $6x+2y+3z=9.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=0$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}6x+2y+3z & =9 \\ 6(1)+2(0)+3z & =9 \\ 3z & =3 \\ z & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get the point $Q(1,0,1)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overset{\to }{PQ},$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨1,0,1⟩-⟨-1,3,-4⟩ \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $n=⟨a,b,c⟩.$ So, for the plane $Π,$ we have $n=⟨6,2,3⟩.$ 

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $Π$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overset{\to }{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =|{\text{comp}}_{n}\,\overset{\to }{PQ}| \\  & =\frac{|\overset{\to }{PQ}\cdot n|}{|n|} \\  & =\frac{|2\cdot 6+(-3)\cdot 2+5\cdot 3|}{\sqrt{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{|12-6+15|}{\sqrt{36+4+9}} \\  & =\frac{|21|}{\sqrt{49}} \\  & =\frac{21}{7} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
